claim: Single-molecule approaches provide enormous insight into the dynamics of biomolecules, but adequately sampling distributions of states and events often requires extensive sampling.
source: Single-molecule approaches provide enormous insight into the dynamics of biomolecules, but adequately sampling distributions of states and events often requires extensive sampling.
evidence: This is a general statement about single-molecule approaches that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Emerging experimental techniques can generate large datasets of single-molecule data.
source: Although emerging experimental techniques can generate such large datasets, existing analysis tools are not suitable to process the large volume of data obtained in high-throughput paradigms.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to technological advances discussed in the introduction section.

claim: Existing analysis tools are not suitable to process the large volume of data obtained in high-throughput paradigms.
source: Although emerging experimental techniques can generate such large datasets, existing analysis tools are not suitable to process the large volume of data obtained in high-throughput paradigms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the discussion of computational bottlenecks in the introduction and by comparative performance data shown in the results.

claim: DISC idealizes single-molecule trajectories up to three orders of magnitude faster than other commonly used algorithms.
source: By merging model-free statistical learning with the Viterbi algorithm, DISC idealizes single-molecule trajectories up to three orders of magnitude faster with improved accuracy compared to other commonly used algorithms.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational performance data presented in Figure 4a showing speed comparisons.

claim: DISC provides improved accuracy compared to other commonly used algorithms.
source: By merging model-free statistical learning with the Viterbi algorithm, DISC idealizes single-molecule trajectories up to three orders of magnitude faster with improved accuracy compared to other commonly used algorithms.
evidence: This claim is supported by accuracy measurements presented in Figure 3a comparing DISC to STaSI and vbFRET.

claim: DISC was used to probe cooperativity between multiple binding events in the cyclic nucleotide binding domains of HCN pacemaker channel.
source: Further, we demonstrate the utility of DISC algorithm to probe cooperativity between multiple binding events in the cyclic nucleotide binding domains of HCN pacemaker channel.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental application described in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Single-molecule methods are powerful tools for providing insight into heterogeneous dynamics underlying chemical and biological processes otherwise obscured in bulk-averaged measurements.
source: Single-molecule methods are powerful tools for providing insight into heterogeneous dynamics underlying chemical and biological processes otherwise obscured in bulk-averaged measurements (Moerner et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moerner et al., 2015.

claim: Use of single-molecule techniques has expanded rapidly, with modalities spanning electrophysiology, fluorescence, and force spectroscopy.
source: Use of these techniques has expanded rapidly, with modalities spanning electrophysiology, fluorescence, and force spectroscopy to probe diverse physical phenomena.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: There is an increasing demand for high-throughput technologies to adequately sample different sub-populations and rare but important events.
source: Following the growing realization that molecules involved in physiological and chemical processes exhibit complex kinetics and a diversity of behavior, there is an increasing demand for high-throughput technologies to adequately sample different sub-populations and rare but important events (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2017.

claim: The observation window prior to photobleaching in conventional fluorescence paradigms can be dramatically extended with recently developed photostable dyes.
source: For example, the observation window prior to photobleaching in conventional fluorescence paradigms such as single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) or colocalization single-molecule spectroscopy (CoSMoS) can be dramatically extended with recently developed photostable dyes (Grimm et al., 2015; Altman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grimm et al., 2015 and Altman et al., 2012.

claim: The current generation of sCMOS detectors enables simultaneous imaging of 1 × 10^4 molecules in a TIRFM configuration.
source: The current generation of metal-oxide semiconductor (sCMOS) detectors enables simultaneous imaging of 1 × 104 molecules in a total internal fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) configuration and can be coupled with nanofabricated zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs) to enable access to high concentrations (Levene et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Juette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levene et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Juette et al., 2016.

claim: sCMOS detectors can be coupled with nanofabricated zero-mode waveguides to enable access to high concentrations.
source: The current generation of metal-oxide semiconductor (sCMOS) detectors enables simultaneous imaging of 1 × 104 molecules in a total internal fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM) configuration and can be coupled with nanofabricated zero-mode waveguides (ZMWs) to enable access to high concentrations (Levene et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Juette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Levene et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2014; Juette et al., 2016.

claim: Non-fluorescence-based single-molecule experiments generate a tremendous amount of data through parallel measurement of hundreds of molecules with orders of magnitude longer recordings than typical fluorescence experiments.
source: Non-fluorescence-based single-molecule experiments such as plasmon rulers, scattering, magnetic tweezers, and single-molecule centrifugation generate a tremendous amount of data through parallel measurement of hundreds of molecules with orders of magnitude longer recordings than a typical fluorescence experiment (Berghuis et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016; Popa et al., 2016; Young and Kukura, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berghuis et al., 2016; Ye et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2016; Popa et al., 2016; Young and Kukura, 2019.

claim: Standard analysis algorithms impose a computational bottleneck at the scale of high-throughput data generation.
source: Unfortunately, despite these advances in generating statistically robust data sets, standard analysis algorithms impose a computational bottleneck at this scale of data generation (Hill et al., 2017; Juette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hill et al., 2017 and Juette et al., 2016.

claim: The computational bottleneck is particularly true when the dynamics and physical states of a system are unknown.
source: This is particularly true when the dynamics and physical states of a system are unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of unsupervised vs supervised analysis methods.

claim: Hidden Markov models model a molecule's behavior as a Markov chain, wherein the molecule transitions between hidden discrete states whose outputs are measured experimentally.
source: The first is a probabilistic approach that models a molecule's behavior as a Markov chain, wherein the molecule transitions between hidden discrete states whose outputs are measured experimentally (hidden Markov model, HMM).
evidence: This is a description of established HMM methodology in the field.

claim: Numerous software packages have been developed for implementing HMMs, including QuB, HaMMy, SMART, vbFRET, ebFRET and SPARTAN.
source: Numerous software packages have been developed for implementing HMMs, such as QuB (Nicolai and Sachs, 2013; Qin et al., 2000), HaMMy (McKinney et al., 2006), SMART (Greenfeld et al., 2012), vbFRET (Bronson et al., 2009), ebFRET (van de Meent et al., 2014) and SPARTAN (Juette et al., 2016), each of which utilize a different HMM training method.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the respective software packages.

claim: QuB implements the fast segmental k-means algorithm which combines k-means clustering and the Viterbi algorithm.
source: For example, QuB implements the fast segmental k-means algorithm (SKM) which combines k-means clustering and the Viterbi algorithm to identify transitions between postulated states (Juang and Rabiner, 1990), whereas vbFRET adapts variational Bayesian inference for parameter estimation at faster speeds than traditional HMM training in both smFRET and single-particle tracking experiments (Blanco and Walter, 2010; Persson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Juang and Rabiner, 1990.

claim: vbFRET adapts variational Bayesian inference for parameter estimation at faster speeds than traditional HMM training.
source: For example, QuB implements the fast segmental k-means algorithm (SKM) which combines k-means clustering and the Viterbi algorithm to identify transitions between postulated states (Juang and Rabiner, 1990), whereas vbFRET adapts variational Bayesian inference for parameter estimation at faster speeds than traditional HMM training in both smFRET and single-particle tracking experiments (Blanco and Walter, 2010; Persson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blanco and Walter, 2010 and Persson et al., 2013.

claim: HMMs have notable limitations, especially in the context of high-throughput analysis and unknown system dynamics.
source: Although powerful statistical tools are very useful for single-molecule analysis, HMMs have notable limitations, especially in the context of high-throughput analysis and unknown system dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of HMM limitations throughout the introduction.

claim: HMMs are often used in a supervised manner where the user postulates model parameters such as the number of states, their measured outputs, and the allowed transitions between them.
source: For example, HMMs are often used in a supervised manner where the user postulates model parameters such as the number of states, their measured outputs, and the allowed transitions between them.
evidence: This describes common practice in HMM application based on established knowledge.

claim: Testing multiple HMM models and ranking them can dramatically increase the analysis time.
source: This process can dramatically increase the analysis time to ensure the parameters space has been sufficiently explored, which restrict their usefulness in high-throughput single-molecule analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational complexity of model selection procedures.

claim: Infinite HMMs using Bayesian nonparametric inference are often computationally prohibitive for large data sets.
source: Although variants such as infinite HMMs using Bayesian nonparametric inference try to naturally learn the trajectory of the states without the typical parametric model selection, these too are often computationally prohibitive for large data sets (Hines et al., 2015; Sgouralis and Pressé, 2017; Sgouralis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hines et al., 2015; Sgouralis and Pressé, 2017; Sgouralis et al., 2018.

claim: Hierarchical agglomerative clustering algorithms begin by treating each observation as singleton clusters and perform N-1 iterations wherein pairs of clusters are merged.
source: Typically, clusters of intensity values (e.g. states) are determined using bottom-up hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) algorithms, which begin by treating each observation of N total observations as singleton clusters and perform N-1 iterations wherein pairs of clusters are merged until all data-points belong to a single cluster.
evidence: This describes the established methodology of HAC algorithms.

claim: Bottom-up hierarchical agglomerative clustering has time complexity of O(N^2) owing to the need of computing a NxN similarity matrix.
source: This implementation results in time complexity of O(N2) owning to the need of computing a NxN similarity matrix to determine which clusters should be merged at each iteration.
evidence: This is based on established computational complexity analysis of HAC algorithms.

claim: Change-point detection precedes HAC to reduce the solution domain of the objective function by identifying statistically significant stepwise changes in signal over time.
source: In practice, a separate algorithm called change-point (CP) detection precedes HAC to reduce the solution domain of the objective function by identifying statistically significant stepwise changes in signal over time.
evidence: This describes the established CP-HAC methodology.

claim: STaSI uses the Student's t-test for fast CP detection and minimum description length for state selection.
source: Variants of this framework such as STaSI use other merit functions for Gaussian noise, including the Student's t-test for fast CP detection and minimum description length for state selection (Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shuang et al., 2014.

claim: CP-HAC methods offer superior computational speed over HMM approaches in common experimental modalities such as smFRET.
source: In common experimental modalities such as smFRET, CP-HAC methods offer superior computational speed over HMM approaches; however, their quadratic time-complexity renders them inefficient on long trajectories (Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shuang et al., 2014.

claim: The quadratic time-complexity of CP-HAC methods renders them inefficient on long trajectories.
source: In common experimental modalities such as smFRET, CP-HAC methods offer superior computational speed over HMM approaches; however, their quadratic time-complexity renders them inefficient on long trajectories (Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shuang et al., 2014 and computational complexity analysis.

claim: Simulation studies have suggested CP-HAC algorithms yield lower event detection accuracy than HMM approaches.
source: In addition, simulation studies have suggested CP-HAC algorithms yield lower event detection accuracy than HMM approaches (Hadzic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hadzic et al., 2018.

claim: DISC uses divisive clustering to allocate data points into states in a top-down process.
source: We advance these ideas by adapting divisive clustering algorithms from data mining and information theory to improve the rate and accuracy of identifying signal amplitude clusters (states) in a top-down process as opposed to the typical bottom-up clustering (Pelleg and Moore, 2000; Karypis et al., 2000; Hamerly and Elkan, 2003).
evidence: This describes the methodology of DISC and is supported by citations to divisive clustering literature.

claim: DISC couples model-free state detection with the Viterbi algorithm to enable robust event detection.
source: We further couple our model-free state detection with the Viterbi algorithm to enable robust event detection on par with HMM methods (Juang and Rabiner, 1990; Qin, 2004; Viterbi, 1967).
evidence: This describes the methodology of DISC and is supported by citations to Viterbi algorithm literature.

claim: DISC is an unsupervised method that combines statistical learning approaches with the high event detection accuracy of HMMs at a fraction of the computational cost.
source: Overall, DISC is an unsupervised method that combines statistical learning approaches with the high event detection accuracy of HMMs at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling convenient application to large datasets.
evidence: This claim is supported by performance data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The goal of the DISC algorithm is time series idealization: the hard assignment of data points into discrete states.
source: The goal of the DISC algorithm is time series idealization: the hard assignment of data points into discrete states.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the algorithm's objective.

claim: DISC approaches idealization as an unsupervised problem in machine learning wherein the number of significant states for a given single-molecule trajectory are not known a priori.
source: DISC approaches the problem of idealization as an unsupervised problem in machine learning wherein the number of significant states for a given single-molecule trajectory are not known a priori.
evidence: This describes the fundamental approach of DISC.

claim: DISC accomplishes idealization in three phases: divisive segmentation, HAC, and the Viterbi algorithm.
source: This process of learning both the significant states and the transitions between them is accomplished in three phases: 1) divisive segmentation, 2) HAC, and 3) the Viterbi algorithm (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the methodology shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Divisive clustering initializes all data-points to a single cluster and iteratively splits data into sub-clusters until each data point is its own singleton cluster.
source: Divisive clustering initializes all data-points to a single cluster and iteratively splits data into sub-clusters until each data point is its own singleton cluster.
evidence: This describes the established methodology of divisive clustering.

claim: There are 2^(N-1)-1 ways of splitting N data points into two sub-clusters.
source: Given that there are 2 N−1-1 ways of spitting N data points into two sub-clusters, the complexity of top-down processes has led to their infrequent use.
evidence: This is based on combinatorial mathematics.

claim: Efficient implementations of divisive clustering using k-means and objective functions can reach O(N) time complexity.
source: In addition, when using k-means for partitioning data points into sub-clusters, the top-down algorithms can reach O(N) time complexity (Karypis et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Karypis et al., 2000.

claim: The first phase of DISC is divisive segmentation.
source: The first phase of DISC is divisive segmentation.
evidence: This describes the structure of the DISC algorithm.

claim: Divisive segmentation allocates each data-point into two unique states through CP detection and k-means clustering.
source: Allocating each data-point into two unique states is accomplished in two sequential phases: CP detection and k-means clustering.
evidence: This describes the methodology of divisive segmentation in DISC.

claim: CP detection is performed with the recursive binary segmentation algorithm.
source: CP detection is performed with the popular recursive binary segmentation algorithm (Watkins and Yang, 2005; Scott and Knott, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watkins and Yang, 2005 and Scott and Knott, 1974.

claim: DISC uses a two-way Student's t-test of unequal sample size but uniform variance to evaluate differences in mean between segments.
source: To determine whether there is a statistically significant difference between the two segments, we use a two-way Student's t-test of unequal sample size but uniform variance to evaluate the differences in mean. This is the same approach used in STaSI (Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in DISC and is supported by a citation to Shuang et al., 2014.

claim: DISC uses a modified k-means algorithm that is both deterministic and faster than standard implementations through use of triangle inequality.
source: For efficiency, DISC uses a modified k-means algorithm that is both deterministic and faster than standard implementations through use of triangle inequality for computational reduction (Elkan, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Elkan, 2003.

claim: DISC uses the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) to determine if data is better fit with one or two states.
source: To determine whether one or two states provides a better fit, we use the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) which is defined in a general form as
evidence: This describes the methodology used in DISC.

claim: The recursive bi-partitioning and binary decision making in both CP detection and divisive clustering result in a reduced time complexity on the order of O(Nlog(N)).
source: Overall, the recursive bi-partitioning and binary decision making in both CP detection and divisive clustering result in a reduced time complexity on the order of O(Nlog(N)).
evidence: This is based on computational complexity analysis of the DISC algorithm.

claim: Over-fitting the number of states in divisive segmentation results from a downward dissemination of error from early splits.
source: Over-fitting the number of states results from a downward dissemination of error from early splits: if bisecting a given cluster is suboptimal, two different parent clusters may each produce highly similar and redundant sub-clusters thereby overfitting the number of states.
evidence: This is an inference about the behavior of divisive segmentation based on algorithmic analysis.

claim: The second phase of DISC uses HAC to compute similarities between all identified states at a global level.
source: Therefore, the second phase of DISC uses HAC to compute the similarities between all identified states at a global level and assess the fit of the whole trajectory rather than segmented portions.
evidence: This describes the methodology of DISC.

claim: Divisive segmentation alone tends to slightly over-estimate the number of states.
source: Although divisive segmentation alone tends to slightly over-estimate the number of states, it provides a more reasonable estimate than CP detection alone (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Divisive segmentation provides a more reasonable estimate of the number of states than CP detection alone.
source: Although divisive segmentation alone tends to slightly over-estimate the number of states, it provides a more reasonable estimate than CP detection alone (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: CP detection alone is very fast but consistently yields a higher number of total states compared to the ground truth.
source: While CP detection alone (Figure 2b, blue) is very fast, it consistently yields a higher number of total states as compared to the ground truth.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CP-HAC frameworks can achieve higher accuracy than CP detection alone, but they are much slower algorithms.
source: As CP-HAC frameworks must explore this large state space in its entirety, they can achieve higher accuracy than CP detection alone, but they are much slower algorithms (Figure 2b, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The use of top-down clustering in divisive segmentation dramatically reduces the total state-space for exploration, resulting in a faster algorithm than CP-HAC with much higher accuracy than CP detection alone.
source: In contrast, the use of top-down clustering in divisive segmentation dramatically reduces the total state-space for exploration, resulting in a faster algorithm than CP-HAC with much higher accuracy than CP detection alone (Figure 2b, purple).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The sequential combination of divisive segmentation and HAC used in DISC leads to the highest state detection accuracy with minimal computational cost.
source: Finally, the sequential combination of divisive segmentation and HAC used in DISC lead to the highest state detection accuracy with minimal computational cost (Figure 2b, orange).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Results from CP detection alone were accurate for slower events, but often failed to identify faster transitions.
source: As shown previously (Hadzic et al., 2018), we found that results from CP detection alone were accurate for slower events, but often failed to identify faster transitions (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d and a citation to Hadzic et al., 2018.

claim: Refining the results of unsupervised clustering with the Viterbi algorithm significantly improved event detection accuracy over CP detection and clustering alone across two-orders of magnitude of varying koff.
source: By refining the results of unsupervised clustering with the Viterbi algorithm, we found that event detection accuracy was significantly improved over CP detection and clustering alone across two-orders of magnitude of varying koff (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The Viterbi algorithm identifies the most probable sequence of hidden states through a series of observations.
source: The goal of the Viterbi algorithm is to identify the most probable sequence of hidden states through a series of observations.
evidence: This describes the established function of the Viterbi algorithm.

claim: The Viterbi algorithm uses dynamic programming to store only the most optimal state sequencing leading up to a given time point.
source: A solution to this problem is the Viterbi algorithm, which makes use of dynamics programming to store only the most optimal state sequencing leading up to a given time point.
evidence: This describes the established methodology of the Viterbi algorithm.

claim: The time complexity of idealization with Viterbi is quadratic in the number of states K and linear with the number of observations N, O(K^2N).
source: Therefore, the time complexity of idealization with Viterbi is quadratic in the number of states K and linear with the number of observations N, O(K2N), which is dramatically lower than an exhaustive search.
evidence: This is based on computational complexity analysis of the Viterbi algorithm.

claim: DISC has been intentionally developed as a flexible framework for adaptation to different types of data.
source: While the parameters used above are valid for trajectories with Gaussian noise, we do not claim they are optimal for all experimental modalities. We have intentionally developed DISC as a flexible framework for adaptation to different types of data.
evidence: This describes the design philosophy of DISC.

claim: The harsh penalty for parameters in BIC can lead to underfitting in certain cases.
source: For example, the harsh penalty for parameters in BIC can lead to underfitting in certain cases; therefore, less stringent Akaike information criterion (AIC) or Hannan-Quinn information criterion (HQC) may be more appropriate depending on the separation of states and noise (Akaike, 1974; Hannan and Quinn, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Akaike, 1974 and Hannan and Quinn, 1979.

claim: DISC performs idealization through unsupervised clustering, but obtaining accurate results requires the user to determine the appropriate information criterion and CP detection methods.
source: It is important to note that while DISC performs idealization through unsupervised clustering, obtaining accurate results does require the user to determine the appropriate information criterion and CP detection methods as idealization results heavily depend on these variables.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for using DISC effectively.

claim: The central innovation of DISC is to take advantage of the best features of both top-down and bottom-up forms of cluster identification that leads to both fast and accurate state detection.
source: Critically, the central innovation of DISC is to take advantage of the best features of both top-down and bottom-up forms of cluster identification that leads to both fast and accurate state detection.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the key innovation of DISC.

claim: Simulated single-molecule trajectories were generated using kinetic parameters obtained from studies exploring the regulatory mechanisms of cyclic nucleotide binding domains from HCN channels.
source: We validate DISC using simulated single-molecule trajectories using kinetic parameters obtained from our recent studies exploring the regulatory mechanisms of cyclic nucleotide binding domains (CNBDs) from hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels (HCN) which regulate pacemaking in heart and brain cells (Materials and methods) (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2017; Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2017 and Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016.

claim: Trajectories obtained with CoSMoS exhibit heterogeneous bound intensity values which vary with each binding event.
source: Notably, trajectories obtained with CoSMoS exhibit heterogeneous bound intensity values which vary with each binding event (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The heterogeneous intensity fluctuation is likely caused by shifts of the molecule in the heterogeneous excitation field of the ZMW or dye photodynamics.
source: While we are uncertain as to the exact source of this fluctuation, it is likely caused by shifts of the molecule in the heterogeneous excitation field of the ZMW or dye photodynamics (Levene et al., 2003; Dempsey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Levene et al., 2003 and Dempsey et al., 2009.

claim: TIRF and confocal microscopy also contain a heterogenous excitation field.
source: While the excitation field changes particularly sharply in ZMWs, TIRF and confocal microscopy also contain a heterogenous excitation field (Moerner and Fromm, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moerner and Fromm, 2003.

claim: Heterogeneous intensity values are a common and inconvenient feature in real life single-molecule fluorescence data.
source: Thus, heterogeneous intensity values are a common and inconvenient feature in real life single-molecule fluorescence data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discussion of various sources of intensity heterogeneity.

claim: 4000 trajectories composed of 2000 data points each were simulated, totaling 8 × 10^6 data points.
source: In total, we simulated 4000 trajectories composed of 2000 data points each, totaling 8 × 106 data points.
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters used for validation.

claim: Each simulated trajectory is 200 s in duration collected at frame rate of 10 Hz.
source: Each trajectory is 200 s in duration collected at frame rate of 10 Hz.
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters used for validation.

claim: vbFRET and STaSI were chosen for benchmarking following the results of a recent comparative study that determined these to be the best performers among their class of analysis methods.
source: These algorithms were chosen following the results of a recent comparative study that determined these to be the best performers among their class of analysis methods (Hadzic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hadzic et al., 2018.

claim: DISC, STaSI and vbFRET are all written entirely in MATLAB which standardizes computational performance.
source: In addition, DISC, STaSI and vbFRET all perform trajectory-by-trajectory idealization and are written entirely in MATLAB (MathWorks) which standardizes computational performance (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the implementation details that enable fair comparison.

claim: Across all simulations, DISC provides the highest average accuracy, precision and recall.
source: Across all the simulations, DISC provides the highest average accuracy, precision and recall (Figure 3a, terms defined in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: No algorithm can idealize a trajectory in the presence of SNR = 1.
source: While no algorithm can idealize a trajectory in the presence of SNR = 1, DISC returns the lowest accuracy at SNR = 2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the performance data at very low SNR.

claim: DISC returns the lowest accuracy at SNR = 2, likely due to the use of robust BIC for state detection.
source: While no algorithm can idealize a trajectory in the presence of SNR = 1, DISC returns the lowest accuracy at SNR = 2. We suspect this result is due to the use of robust BIC for state detection; accuracy would likely be improved with less penalizing objective functions, such as AIC.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of lower performance at SNR = 2.

claim: For SNR > 3, DISC performs exceptionally well with highest average accuracy (0.91 ± 0.05) and is robust against false positives (precision = 0.96 ± 0.04) and false negatives (recall = 0.93 ± 0.03).
source: For SNR > 3, which accounts for most of our experimentally obtained data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), DISC performs exceptionally well with highest average accuracy (0.91 ± 0.05) and is robust against false positives (precision = 0.96 ± 0.04) and false negatives (recall = 0.93 ± 0.03) across all simulated conditions (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: vbFRET matches the recall of DISC in the SNR > 3 range (0.94 ± 0.05), but the tendency to overfit the number of states at higher SNR lowers precision (0.80 ± 0.18) and overall accuracy (0.76 ± 0.19).
source: While vbFRET matches the recall of DISC in this SNR range (0.94 ± 0.05), the tendency to overfit the number of states at higher SNR lowers precision (0.80 ± 0.18) and overall accuracy (0.76 ± 0.19).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: STaSI returns the lowest overall accuracy (0.47 ± 0.17) likely due to overfitting the number of states (precision = 0.57 ± 0.2) and a tendency to miss transitions (recall = 0.75 ± 0.10).
source: We find STaSI returns the lowest overall accuracy (0.47 ± 0.17) likely do to an overfitting the number of states (precision = 0.57 ± 0.2) and a tendency to miss transitions (recall = 0.75 ± 0.10).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: DISC is the only method unaffected by inclusion of heterogeneous state intensities of fcAMP likely due to the use of a Gaussian derived BIC for state selection.
source: Notably, DISC is the only method unaffected by inclusion of heterogeneous state intensities of fcAMP likely due to the use of a Gaussian derived BIC for state selection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Idealization of all 4000 trajectories by DISC was completed in just over two minutes.
source: Critically, DISC not only returned high accuracy results, DISC was also much faster than the other methods. Idealization of all 4000 trajectories by DISC was completed in just over two minutes, whereas STaSI took over fifteen minutes and vbFRET took over twelve hours.
evidence: This describes the computational performance of DISC on the validation dataset.

claim: STaSI took over fifteen minutes to idealize all 4000 trajectories.
source: Critically, DISC not only returned high accuracy results, DISC was also much faster than the other methods. Idealization of all 4000 trajectories by DISC was completed in just over two minutes, whereas STaSI took over fifteen minutes and vbFRET took over twelve hours.
evidence: This describes the computational performance of STaSI on the validation dataset.

claim: vbFRET took over twelve hours to idealize all 4000 trajectories.
source: Critically, DISC not only returned high accuracy results, DISC was also much faster than the other methods. Idealization of all 4000 trajectories by DISC was completed in just over two minutes, whereas STaSI took over fifteen minutes and vbFRET took over twelve hours.
evidence: This describes the computational performance of vbFRET on the validation dataset.

claim: DISC is 400-fold to 1,200-fold faster than vbFRET.
source: Remarkably, we find DISC is 400-fold to 1,200-fold faster than vbFRET and 2-fold to 8,700-fold faster than STaSI due to STaSI's quadratic time dependence (Figure 4a; Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a and a citation to Shuang et al., 2014.

claim: DISC is 2-fold to 8,700-fold faster than STaSI due to STaSI's quadratic time dependence.
source: Remarkably, we find DISC is 400-fold to 1,200-fold faster than vbFRET and 2-fold to 8,700-fold faster than STaSI due to STaSI's quadratic time dependence (Figure 4a; Shuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a and a citation to Shuang et al., 2014.

claim: A trajectory of 10^6 data points can be analyzed by DISC in 10 s compared to 3 hr for vbFRET and 27 hr for STaSI.
source: For example, a trajectory of 106 data points can be analyzed by DISC in 10 s compared to 3 hr for vbFRET and 27 hr for STaSI.
evidence: This is an example calculation based on the performance data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: For simulations featuring two or three states FRET, DISC is 5.5-fold faster than STaSI and 235-fold faster than vbFRET while maintaining the highest accuracy.
source: For simulations featuring two or three states FRET, we find DISC 5.5-fold faster than STaSI and 235-fold faster than vbFRET while maintaining the highest accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The accuracy of DISC increases with increasing number of data points per trajectory.
source: As expected, we find that the accuracy increases with increasing number of data points per trajectory. This result also indicates the minimum number of data points needed for an accurate idealization for a given SNR (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Previous macroscopic studies of HCN channel gating have revealed that ligand binding to CNBDs exhibits both positive and negative cooperativity depending on the ligation state and the membrane potential.
source: Previous macroscopic studies of HCN channel gating have revealed that ligand binding to CNBDs exhibits both positive and negative cooperativity depending on the ligation state and the membrane potential (Kusch et al., 2012; Thon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kusch et al., 2012 and Thon et al., 2015.

claim: Cyclic AMP regulates cardiac pacemaking via HCN channels.
source: Cyclic AMP regulates cardiac pacemaking via HCN channels and, therefore, this unusual allostery has significant physiological implications.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HCN channel function.

claim: The initial dataset included 13,670 ZMWs each monitored for 800 s at a sampling rate of 10 Hz.
source: Our initial dataset included 13,670 ZMWs each monitored for 800 s at a sampling rate of 10 Hz (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental dataset used for analysis.

claim: All trajectories were obtained in the presence of 1 µM fcAMP which is near the ligand dissociation constant for individual CNBDs.
source: All trajectories were obtained in the presence of 1 µM fcAMP which is near the ligand dissociation constant for individual CNBDs (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016.

claim: DISC successfully processed the entire dataset of 13,670 trajectories within 20 min using a standard MacBook Air.
source: Therefore, we first analyzed all trajectories with DISC to find reliable data prior to trace selection. DISC successfully processed this entire data set within 20 min using a standard MacBook Air (1.6 GHz Intel Core i5).
evidence: This describes the computational performance of DISC on the experimental dataset.

claim: The same analysis completed with STaSI yielded unphysical results in 4 hr.
source: The same analysis completed with STaSI yielded unphysical results in 4 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis with vbFRET was estimated to take weeks to complete and was therefore not performed.
source: We estimated analysis with vbFRET would take weeks to complete and was therefore not performed.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the computational performance of vbFRET on smaller datasets.

claim: The passivated surfaces within the ZMWs greatly reduce non-specific absorption of fcAMP to either the metallic or glass surfaces.
source: While correcting for non-specific binding is often a necessity in CoSMoS experiments, we find the passivated surfaces within the ZMWs greatly reduce non-specific absorption of fcAMP to either the metallic or glass surfaces, thus minimizing this concern (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Smith et al., 2019; Eid et al., 2009; Foquet et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citations to Smith et al., 2019; Eid et al., 2009; Foquet et al., 2008.

claim: An asynchronous decay of protein activity over excitation time was observed that may be caused by singlet-oxygen formation and subsequent inhibition of cyclic nucleotide binding to CNBDs.
source: Notably, we noticed an asynchronous decay of protein activity over excitation time that may be caused by singlet-oxygen formation and subsequent inhibition of cyclic nucleotide binding to CNBDs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Idikuda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and a citation to Idikuda et al., 2018.

claim: 293 molecules totaling 1.2 × 10^5 s of combined protein activity across 53,474 events were retained for analysis.
source: In conclusion, we retained 293 molecules totaling 1.2 × 105 s of combined protein activity across 53,474 events.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used for analysis after trace selection.

claim: The binomial fit of state occupancies matches the distribution well and returns the probability of occupancy at 1 µM fcAMP for a single CNBD in the tetramer as 31%.
source: Our binomial fit matches the distribution well and returns the probability of occupancy at 1 µM fcAMP for a single CNBD in the tetramer as 31% which is similar to our previous monomeric CNBDs studies (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016), suggesting a lack of cooperativity between the CNBDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the binomial fit shown in Figure 5c and a citation to Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016.

claim: The probability of occupancy at 1 µM fcAMP for a single CNBD in the tetramer is similar to previous monomeric CNBDs studies, suggesting a lack of cooperativity between the CNBDs.
source: Our binomial fit matches the distribution well and returns the probability of occupancy at 1 µM fcAMP for a single CNBD in the tetramer as 31% which is similar to our previous monomeric CNBDs studies (Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016), suggesting a lack of cooperativity between the CNBDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison to previous data cited from Goldschen-Ohm et al., 2016.

claim: The measured state-occupancy distribution is strikingly different than the unusual cooperativity modeled from either activated or non-activated channels.
source: Notably, our measured state-occupancy distribution is strikingly different that than the unusual cooperativity modeled from either activated or non-activated channels (Figure 5—figure supplement 5; Kusch et al., 2012; Thon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5 and citations to Kusch et al., 2012 and Thon et al., 2015.

claim: The optimized kon and koff rates for each state transition exhibit a strong linear relationship, as expected for non-cooperative processes.
source: As expected for non-cooperative processes, the optimized kon and koff rates for each state transition exhibit a strong linear relationship (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The results strongly suggest that CNBD units act independently during ligand binding.
source: Combined, these results strongly suggest that CNBD units act independently during ligand binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binomial distribution fit and linear relationship of rate constants.

claim: The macroscopically observed cooperativity is either an artifact of model fitting or requires the presence of the transmembrane domains of the HCN channel and is not an intrinsic property of the CNBDs.
source: We postulate that the macroscopically observed cooperativity is either an artifact of model fitting or that it requires the presence of the transmembrane domains of the HCN channel and is not an intrinsic property of the CNBDs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: DISC combines unsupervised statistical learning of discrete states with the event detection power of the Viterbi algorithm to quickly identify both significant states and transitions in a model-independent manner.
source: We developed a new algorithm for rapid and accurate unsupervised idealization of single-molecule trajectories. Our approach combines unsupervised statistical learning of discrete states with the event detection power of the Viterbi algorithm to quickly identify both significant states and transitions in a model-independent manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the DISC algorithm's approach.

claim: Software implementing the DISC algorithm that includes a graphical user interface is available at https://github.com/ChandaLab/DISC.
source: Software implementing the DISC algorithm that includes a graphical user interface is available at https://github.com/ChandaLab/DISC (Chanda et al., 2019; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/DISC).
evidence: This provides information about software availability.

claim: DISC is not a fully probabilistic approach.
source: Like CP-HAC methods, DISC is not a fully probabilistic approach.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the DISC algorithm.

claim: Fully probabilistic HMM training approaches provide unbiased estimates of parameter distributions but at the cost of significantly increased computational time.
source: While fully probabilistic HMM training approaches are beneficial for providing unbiased estimates of the parameter distributions, their high accuracy comes at the cost of significantly increased computational time.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HMM training methods.

claim: Recently developed infinite HMM approaches can take days to analyze single trajectories.
source: However, accomplishing this task costs hundreds of iterations per trace to provide a reproducible fit with some approaches taking days to analyze single trajectories (Hines et al., 2015; Sgouralis and Pressé, 2017; Sgouralis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hines et al., 2015; Sgouralis and Pressé, 2017; Sgouralis et al., 2018.

claim: Exhaustive search algorithms are clearly not suited for large datasets associated with high-throughput experiments.
source: Thus, while exhaustive search algorithms may be desirable in other contexts, they are clearly not suited for large datasets associated with high-throughput experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational performance comparisons.

claim: DISC surpasses the accuracy of common CP-HAC and HMM algorithms with a dramatic improvement in computational speed.
source: In contrast, by simulating data closely resembling the binding of fcAMP to pacemaker channels, we find that DISC surpasses the accuracy of common CP-HAC and HMM algorithms with a dramatic improvement in computational speed.
evidence: This claim is supported by the performance data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: DISC satisfies the need for accuracy and speed in high-throughput analysis.
source: Therefore, DISC satisfies the need for accuracy and speed in high-throughput analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the performance data.

claim: DISC is like the SKM algorithm for estimating the parameters of an HMM without direct HMM training.
source: In this regard, DISC is like the SKM algorithm for estimating the parameters of an HMM without direct HMM training.
evidence: This is a comparison to another algorithm based on methodological similarities.

claim: Unlike SKM which relies on user-specified states, DISC uses unsupervised statistics to learn the states.
source: However, unlike SKM which relies on user-specified states, DISC uses unsupervised statistics to learn the states.
evidence: This describes a key difference between DISC and SKM.

claim: DISC offers the idealization power of SKM with the state-learning capabilities of CP-HAC.
source: Therefore, DISC offers the idealization power of SKM with the state-learning capabilities of CP-HAC.
evidence: This is a summary of DISC's capabilities relative to other methods.

claim: The rapid and robust idealization provided by DISC enabled stringent trace selection to ensure only reliable trajectories were analyzed.
source: We used DISC to analyze a large dataset obtained from ZMWs to evaluate cooperativity between CNBDs from pacemaker ion channels upon ligand binding. The rapid and robust idealization provided by DISC enabled stringent trace selection to ensure only reliable trajectories were analyzed.
evidence: This describes the application of DISC to the experimental dataset.

claim: In contrast to model inferences from ensemble measurements of HCN2 channels, CNBD tetramers do not exhibit cooperative ligand binding.
source: These data show that, in contrast to model inferences from ensemble measurements of HCN2 channels, CNBD tetramers do not exhibit cooperative ligand binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data analyzed with DISC.

claim: Allosteric interactions between binding sites may be coordinated by the channel's transmembrane domains.
source: This result suggests that allosteric interactions between binding sites may be coordinated by the channel's transmembrane domains.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: The framework of DISC can be easily extended to other data paradigms due to its modular nature.
source: Although we have demonstrated the use of DISC on single-molecule fluorescence data, the framework can be easily extended to other data paradigms due to its modular nature.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of DISC for different applications.

claim: The provided software and GUI allows the user to select from several options the desired parameters such as choice of information criteria.
source: To allow for easy comparison of a given data set, the provided software and graphical user interface (GUI) allows the user to select from several options the desired parameters such as choice of information criteria.
evidence: This describes features of the DISC software.

claim: DISC's flexibility makes it suitable for a wide array of experimental data provided it can be described as a series of transitions between discrete states.
source: This flexibility makes DISC suitable for a wide array of experimental data provided it can be described as a series of transitions between discrete states, including, for example, single-channel current recordings, force spectroscopy and smFRET.
evidence: This describes the applicability of DISC to different experimental modalities.

claim: There is no inherent knowledge within DISC to consider various sources of experimental noise, such as photo-blinking or baseline drift.
source: However, there is no inherent knowledge within DISC to consider various sources of experimental noise, such as photo-blinking or baseline drift; therefore, correcting for these noise sources prior to DISC analysis will likely improve idealization accuracy.
evidence: This describes a limitation of DISC.

claim: Correcting for noise sources such as photo-blinking or baseline drift prior to DISC analysis will likely improve idealization accuracy.
source: However, there is no inherent knowledge within DISC to consider various sources of experimental noise, such as photo-blinking or baseline drift; therefore, correcting for these noise sources prior to DISC analysis will likely improve idealization accuracy.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations of DISC.

claim: DISC provides a dramatic improvement in computational speed over current state-of-the-art approaches while either improving or maintaining high accuracy for both state determination and event detection.
source: Finally, our results show that DISC provides a dramatic improvement in computational speed over current state-of-the-art approaches while either improving or maintaining high accuracy for both state determination and event detection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the performance data.

claim: The increase in speed provided by DISC is directly applicable to analyzing the growing datasets obtained in single-molecule fluorescence paradigms to adequately sample population dynamics.
source: This increase in speed is directly applicable to analyzing the growing datasets obtained in single-molecule fluorescence paradigms to adequately sample population dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference about the applicability of DISC.

claim: The use of sCMOS camera enables smFRET measurements of tRNA conformational changes during protein translations across thousands of molecules simultaneously with millisecond resolution.
source: For example, the use of sCMOS camera enables smFRET measurements of tRNA conformational changes during protein translations across thousands of molecules simultaneously with millisecond resolution (Juette et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Juette et al., 2016.

claim: Magnetic tweezers have enabled week-long mechanical measurements of single-protein folding and unfolding, shifting observable dynamics to pathological time-scales and allowing the detection of rare events.
source: Additionally, magnetic tweezers have enabled week-long mechanical measurements of single-protein folding and unfolding, shifting observable dynamics to pathological time-scales and allowing the detection of rare events (Popa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Popa et al., 2016.

claim: Highly computationally efficient and robust algorithms such as DISC may be well suited for analysis of a wide variety of single molecule datasets beyond the standard smFRET data.
source: Thus, highly computationally efficient and robust algorithms such as DISC may be well suited for analysis of a wide variety of single molecule datasets beyond the standard smFRET data.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential applications of DISC.
